plain: The claim is that something struck the Earth at the time of the Younger Dryas, a sudden return to ice-age cold roughly 12,000 years ago, and that this caused the great flood remembered in old stories and wiped out an earlier civilization. The comedian and interviewer Joe Rogan tells Michels this as his own view. He says that against an impact like that 'you don't have enough to stop that,' and that this is 'probably what happened during the Younger Dryas impact.' Rogan points to old texts: the Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, the ancient Book of Enoch, and the King James Bible of 1611. Michels' co-host, who uses the pseudonym Jack and has spent years working in defense and aerospace, also mentions 'the reset 12,000 years ago.' He credits it to the researchers Randall Carlson and Graham Hancock and names no impact or flood. Rogan does not say which part of Gilgamesh he means. If it is the flood on the Eleventh Tablet, read in E. A. Wallis Budge's 1920 translation, there the great gods resolve 'to make a wind-storm,' 'A black cloud from the foundation of heaven came up,' and the god Adad thunders inside it. Meanwhile the Anunnaki, whom the translator calls star-gods of the southern sky, 'brandished their torches' and 'With their glare they lighted up the land.' That is the tablet's closest image to fire from the sky. Reading the flood as the memory of an impact is a step the tablet neither states nor excludes. If true, the world's flood myths would be memories of a real cosmic catastrophe.

discussion.by: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)
discussion.text: The teller does not say which part of the epic he means; if it is the flood of the Eleventh Tablet, the source says the great gods resolved "to make a wind-storm" and tells a rain-flood, "A black cloud from the foundation of heaven came up" in which Adad thundered, while the Anunnaki, whom the translator glosses as "The star-gods of the southern sky", "brandished their torches" and "With their glare they lighted up the land". Star-gods lighting up the land with torches is the tablet's nearest image to fire from the sky; reading the flood as the memory of an impact is a step the tablet neither states nor excludes. The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood.
